name: Engineering Chemistry Lab
objectives: To provide students with practical knowledge of quantitative analysis of materials and instrumental methods, developing experimental skills and technical competence.
outcomes: To give knowledge of different analytical techniques of chemistry.
To give an idea about volumetric and gravimetric methods of analysis.
To give knowledge about several volumetric methods used in industries like water, hospitals, dyeing, metallurgy etc.
To give an idea about some old and latest instrumental methods of analysis like viscometric, surface tension and conductivity methods.
To give an idea about some useful industrial techniques like chromatography, bomb calorimeter and coal analysis etc.
ref: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ELBS Longman
R.N. Goyal and H. Goel, Engineering Chemistry, An e-publication
note:
Record format: aim, chemicals and apparatus, principle with balanced equation, indicator and end point colour, burette table with three concordant readings (difference 0.1 mL), calculation with N₁V₁ = N₂V₂, result and precautions.
Rinse the burette with the titrant and the pipette with the solution before use; read the lower meniscus at eye level, and write burette readings to 0.05 mL.
Be ready to state the colour change, the pH range of the indicator and why each reagent is used; examiners ask these first.

exps.title: Determination of viscosity by Ostwald viscometer and the molecular weight of a polymer by viscosity measurement
exps.aim: Find the relative viscosity of a liquid and use the intrinsic viscosity of polymer solutions to estimate molecular weight.
exps.apparatus: Ostwald viscometer, stop-watch, thermostat bath, specific gravity bottle, polymer solutions of different concentrations
viva: Why must the viscometer be kept vertical?
Flow time depends on the hydrostatic head, which changes if the tube is tilted.
What is the SI unit of viscosity?
Pa·s (N s m⁻²); in CGS it is poise.
How does temperature affect the viscosity of a liquid?
Viscosity decreases as temperature rises, so a thermostat is required.

exps.title: Determination of surface tension of a liquid by stalagmometer
exps.aim: Find the surface tension of a liquid by comparing drop numbers with water (drop-number method).
exps.apparatus: Stalagmometer, specific gravity bottle, water, test liquid, rubber tube, clamp stand
exps.formula: γ₁/γ₂ = (n₂ρ₁)/(n₁ρ₂) where n = number of drops for the same volume and ρ = density.
viva: Why do drops form?
Surface tension holds the drop until its weight equals the surface-tension force at the tip.
How does temperature affect surface tension?
It decreases as temperature rises.
Why are drops counted for the same fixed volume?
Both liquids must be compared for equal volume so that drop number depends only on γ and ρ.

exps.title: Determination of chloride content of water by Mohr's method
exps.aim: Estimate chloride in a water sample by titration with standard AgNO₃ using K₂CrO₄ indicator.
exps.apparatus: Burette, pipette, conical flask, standard AgNO₃ solution, 5 % K₂CrO₄ indicator, water sample
exps.formula: Cl⁻ + Ag⁺ → AgCl (white); end point: red-brown Ag₂CrO₄. Chloride (mg/L) = (V × N × 35.5 × 1000)/V_sample.
viva: What is the indicator and the end-point colour?
Potassium chromate; the first permanent red-brown Ag₂CrO₄ appears.
Why must the pH lie between 6.5 and 10?
In acid the chromate is converted to dichromate; in strong alkali Ag₂O precipitates.
Why does AgCl precipitate before Ag₂CrO₄?
AgCl is less soluble, so it precipitates first, and Ag₂CrO₄ forms only when chloride is exhausted.

exps.title: Determination of cell constant and conductance of a solution using conductivity meter
exps.aim: Calibrate a conductivity cell with KCl and measure the conductance of a given solution.
exps.apparatus: Conductivity meter, conductivity cell, 0.01 M KCl, given solutions, thermostat, volumetric flasks
exps.formula: Cell constant = l/A = κ/G; κ of 0.01 M KCl is 1.413 mS/cm at 25 °C. Λ = 1000κ/C (κ in S/cm, C in mol/L).
viva: What is the cell constant?
The ratio of electrode separation to electrode area (l/A), in cm⁻¹.
Why is alternating current used?
It prevents electrolysis and polarisation at the electrodes.
How does the conductivity of an electrolyte change with temperature?
It increases, roughly 2 % per °C, as ionic mobility rises.

exps.title: Determination of saponification/acid value of oil
exps.aim: Find the acid value or saponification value of an oil sample by titration.
exps.apparatus: Oil sample, alcoholic KOH, standard HCl or oxalic acid, phenolphthalein, reflux condenser, burette
exps.formula: Acid value = 56.1 × N × V/W (mg KOH per g). Saponification value = 56.1 × N × (B − S)/W; B = blank, S = sample titre.
viva: Define saponification value.
Milligrams of KOH needed to saponify 1 g of oil or fat.
What does a high acid value indicate?
The oil has turned rancid because free fatty acids have formed.
Why is a blank titration run?
It gives the KOH used up without oil, so the difference measures KOH consumed by the oil.

exps.title: Synthesis of aspirin drug in the lab
exps.aim: Prepare aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) from salicylic acid and acetic anhydride, purify it and calculate the yield.
exps.apparatus: Salicylic acid, acetic anhydride, conc. H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄, conical flask, water bath, Buchner funnel, ethanol, ice
exps.formula: C₇H₆O₃ + (CH₃CO)₂O → C₉H₈O₄ + CH₃COOH; M(aspirin) = 180 g/mol; m.p. about 135 °C; % yield = (actual/theoretical) × 100.
viva: What is the role of the acid catalyst?
It activates the acetic anhydride so that the phenolic -OH of salicylic acid is acetylated faster.
How is the purity of aspirin tested?
Ferric chloride gives a purple colour if unreacted salicylic acid (a phenol) remains.
Why is the product recrystallised?
To remove impurities and unreacted salicylic acid, giving pure aspirin crystals.

exps.title: Chemical analysis of a given salt
exps.aim: Identify the anion and cation present in a given simple salt through systematic tests.
exps.apparatus: Salt sample, test tubes, dil. HCl, dil. and conc. H₂SO₄, BaCl₂, AgNO₃, NaOH, NH₄OH, H₂S or thioacetamide, Bunsen burner
exps.formula: Cation groups: I (dil. HCl, Pb²⁺), II (H₂S in acid, Cu²⁺), III (NH₄Cl + NH₄OH, Fe³⁺, Al³⁺), IV (H₂S in alkali, Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺), V ((NH₄)₂CO₃, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺).
viva: Why is NH₄Cl added before NH₄OH for Group III?
It suppresses OH⁻ by the common ion effect so that only Group III hydroxides precipitate.
What is the group reagent for Group I cations?
Dilute hydrochloric acid, which precipitates the chlorides of Pb²⁺, Ag⁺ and Hg₂²⁺.
How is carbonate confirmed?
Dilute acid gives effervescence of CO₂, which turns lime water milky.

exps.title: Determination of the partition coefficient of a solute in two immiscible liquids
exps.aim: Find the distribution coefficient of a solute (e.g. acetic acid or iodine) between two immiscible solvents.
exps.apparatus: Separating funnels, water and organic solvent (benzene or butanol), acetic acid, NaOH, phenolphthalein, burette
exps.formula: K_D = C₁/C₂ (Nernst distribution law), at constant temperature and the same molecular form in both solvents.
viva: State the Nernst distribution law.
At constant temperature, a solute distributes between two immiscible solvents in a constant concentration ratio.
When does the law fail?
When the solute associates or dissociates in one solvent, or the solvents are not immiscible.
What is the use of the law in industry?
Solvent extraction: repeated small extractions remove more solute than one large extraction.

exps.title: Determination of adsorption of acetic acid by charcoal
exps.aim: Verify the Freundlich adsorption isotherm for acetic acid on charcoal.
exps.apparatus: Activated charcoal, acetic acid of varied concentrations, conical flasks, shaker, burette, NaOH, phenolphthalein
exps.formula: x/m = kC^{1/n}, i.e. log(x/m) = log k + (1/n) log C; the plot is a straight line.
viva: What is adsorption?
The accumulation of a substance on the surface of a solid or liquid, unlike absorption which is bulk uptake.
What does the slope of the log-log plot give?
1/n, the adsorption intensity, a value between 0 and 1.
How does temperature affect physical adsorption?
It decreases with a temperature rise, since adsorption is exothermic.

exps.title: Removal of hardness of water by ion exchange column
exps.aim: Demonstrate softening of hard water by passing it through a cation exchange resin and measure hardness before and after.
exps.apparatus: Ion exchange column with cation resin, hard water, EDTA, Eriochrome Black-T, NH₄Cl-NH₄OH buffer, burette
exps.formula: 2R-H + Ca²⁺ → R₂Ca + 2H⁺; regeneration with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄. Hardness (ppm CaCO₃) = (V × M × 100 × 1000)/V_sample.
viva: How does an ion exchanger remove hardness?
The resin exchanges Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in the water for H⁺ or Na⁺ ions.
How is an exhausted cation resin regenerated?
By washing with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ so that H⁺ replaces the retained Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
Why is a cation exchanger followed by an anion exchanger for demineralisation?
The cation resin removes metal ions and the anion resin removes anions, giving demineralised water.

exps.title: Determination of Rf value using paper/thin layer chromatography
exps.aim: Separate the components of a mixture and calculate the Rf value of each.
exps.apparatus: Chromatography paper or TLC plate, developing chamber, solvent, capillary, mixture of amino acids or dyes, ruler
exps.formula: Rf = distance moved by solute / distance moved by solvent front (always less than 1).
viva: Why is Rf always less than 1?
The solute cannot travel farther than the solvent front.
What factors affect Rf?
The solvent system, stationary phase, temperature and the nature of the compound.
How are colourless spots located?
With a spray such as ninhydrin, by iodine vapour, or under UV light.

exps.title: Determination of temporary and permanent hardness of water by complexometric titration
exps.aim: Find total and permanent hardness of water using EDTA and hence calculate temporary hardness.
exps.apparatus: Standard EDTA solution, Eriochrome Black-T, NH₄Cl-NH₄OH buffer (pH 10), burette, pipette, hard water, boiled water
exps.formula: Total hardness (ppm CaCO₃) = (V × M_EDTA × 100 × 1000)/V_sample; temporary = total − permanent.
viva: Why is a buffer of pH 10 used?
EDTA complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ properly and the indicator changes colour sharply at this pH.
What is the end-point colour change?
Wine red to clear blue.
What causes temporary hardness?
Dissolved bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium; boiling removes them.

exps.title: Determination of rate constant of a reaction
exps.aim: Find the first-order rate constant of acid hydrolysis of methyl acetate by titration at different times.
exps.apparatus: Methyl acetate, 0.5 N HCl, standard NaOH, phenolphthalein, ice-cold water, stop-watch, thermostat
exps.formula: k = (2.303/t) log[(V∞ − V₀)/(V∞ − V_t)]; half-life t½ = 0.693/k.
viva: What is the order of the reaction studied?
Pseudo first order, since water is in large excess.
What is the role of HCl?
It acts as a catalyst, while its concentration stays constant.
Why are the samples run into ice-cold water?
This quenches the reaction so that the titre is taken at the required time.

exps.title: To determine the ferrous content in the supplied sample of iron ore by titrimetric analysis against standard K₂Cr₂O₇ solution using K₃Fe(CN)₆ as external indicator
exps.aim: Estimate ferrous iron in an ore solution by titration with standard dichromate, using a spot test for the end point.
exps.apparatus: Iron ore solution, standard K₂Cr₂O₇, K₃Fe(CN)₆ external indicator, white tile, burette, pipette, dil. H₂SO₄
viva: Why is an external indicator used?
Ferricyanide reacts with Fe²⁺ and would consume it if added to the flask, so drops are tested on a tile.
What is the end-point indication?
A drop of the titration mixture no longer gives a blue colour with the indicator.
What is the oxidation state change of chromium?
Cr goes from +6 in dichromate to +3.

exps.title: To determine the constituents and amount of alkalinity of the supplied water sample
exps.aim: Find the hydroxide, carbonate and bicarbonate alkalinity of water using phenolphthalein and methyl orange end points.
exps.apparatus: Water sample, standard H₂SO₄ or HCl, phenolphthalein, methyl orange, burette, pipette, conical flask
exps.formula: P = phenolphthalein titre, M = methyl orange titre. P = 0: HCO₃⁻ only; P = M: OH⁻ only; P = ½M: CO₃²⁻ only; P < ½M: CO₃²⁻ + HCO₃⁻; P > ½M: OH⁻ + CO₃²⁻.
viva: Why can OH⁻ and HCO₃⁻ not coexist?
They react to give carbonate: OH⁻ + HCO₃⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O.
What do the phenolphthalein and methyl orange end points mark?
Phenolphthalein marks about pH 8.3 (OH⁻ and half of CO₃²⁻); methyl orange marks about pH 4.5 (all alkalinity).
Why is alkalinity in water important?
It indicates buffering and scale or corrosion tendency in boilers and pipes.
